item.title: Children of Time by Adrian Czajkowski
item.description: This Czajkowski (Tcaikovsky) is an easy, but long read. Insightful towards how societies evolve and pass knowledge through time. The power in this book is to pose alternatives, just as most science fiction does. There is the standard commentary about how ecological depletion and damage is the scourge that mars this earth, and that systems optimized for one thing, whether it be humans or ants, are not going to result in a happy conclusion. The less standard argument is found in the title, the Children of Time. What does it mean to move through time, and how does moving through time alter the course of events.

item.title: Magnifica Humanitas by Pope Leo XIV
item.description:
The media has dubbed this to be the AI encyclical, but Magnifica Humanitas is more so a porting of Rerum Novarum into the era of automation via digital computers and a lesser extent LLMs (generative AI).

Referencing Benedict XVI, Leo XIV states the capacity of the state is degraded by the capitalization of the market, and thus the ability of the state to address social problems is degraded by increase in privatization of markets. The one aspect which Leo XIV seemed positive about state function was the role in maintaining educational institutions, with an explicit mention of the role of government in education. Other classical functions of state, particularly regulation of markets, were stated as functions of a vague, ‘community’. This implied that the current operations of states are not promoting social objectives of the Church writ large, with the social objective primarily focused on the maintenance of communities. Leo XIV does not have the highest faith in the current institutions which compromise modern states to fulfill the demands of the current moment, particularly with the privatization of social functions by the market and the increasing capitalization of value.

item.title: Vulcan's Hammer by Philip K. Dick
item.description:
A centralized computer runs humanity after a decimating global war.

With this premise, Dick interrogates the effectiveness of withholding information from analysis. Direct information, such as assassinations or riots, should be correlated with economic and social aggregations of data. If the correlations are known beforehand, then the withholding of data leads to a questioning of the reliability of the datasource rather than the proper masking of the sensitive data.

item.title: Kokun: The Girl From the West by Nahoko Uehashi
item.description: Uehashi provides an analysis of empire and agriculture in this fantasy land, asking questions which are similar to those posed by James Scott in Against the Grain. The questions of the state and their role in agrarian systems and enforcing specific agrarian systems above others.

item.title: Dead Souls By Nikolai Gogol
item.description: The title says it all… Well along with the context that Gogol is critiquing the serfdom of the Russian Empire and the legal and financial structures that lead to the emancipation of the surfs. If you want to know more about this, just read the book, it’s a political satire, so it is fun and lighthearted.

item.title: Against the Grain by James Scott
item.description: James Scott gives a foray into a somewhat speculative agriculture of pre-history of Europe and West Asia. The driving premise is that the ‘pre-historical’ agriculture was fairly ecologically stable and widely practiced at the same time as historical agricultural systems. Because the institutions of cities and early states allowed for maintenance of records, our knowledge of historical agricultural systems is biased to preserving agricultural methods which supported cities and states.

item.title: Death and Life of the Great Lakes by Dan Egan
item.description: Invasive species are often portrayed as outside of the ecosystem, as something that unilaterally harms the ecosystem. Dan Egan tries to approach discussing invasive species as a story of history, both human and natural, and evaluate the impacts of invasive species in the great lakes through time and how the role of invasive species changes through time.
